title: Realtime inference & integration PRD (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This doc is an internal PRD draft proposing a combined realtime/interaction surface for the Hosted API focused on three developer pain points: low-latency streaming, first-class tool-calling primitives, and reliable structured output. The goal is an ergonomic SDK and API surface that enables product teams to build interactive features (chat with tools, multi-step flows, structured responses) without ad-hoc glue logic.

Context / background:
- Several customers asked for lower tail latency and better client-side control for interactive UIs (see customer notes in JIRA-API-1021).
- Current REST endpoints support streaming tokens but lack a coherent mechanism for service integration (tool invocation) and for returning validated structured results that downstream services can consume without brittle parsing.
- SDK ergonomics are inconsistent across languages; teams want a single mental model: a stream of events representing model thinking, tool requests, tool results, and final structured outputs.

Primary goals:
1) Define an event-based realtime API that supports streaming tokens, tool-calling events, and final structured responses in a single session stream.
2) Provide SDK primitives (sync/async) that make consuming the event stream easy, with helpers for schema validation and tool adapters.
3) Ensure safe-by-default tool invocation with explicit capability declaration, auditing, and opt-in on a per-customer basis.
4) Do a staged rollout with alpha partners and feature flags, measure quality/regression signals.

Non-goals:
- Not a replacement for batch embedding endpoints or high-throughput non-interactive inference (those remain in dedicated APIs).
- We will not implement an exhaustive tool marketplace in phase 1; phase 1 focuses on first-party tool adapters (HTTP fetch, SQL proxy) and an adapter interface.

User personas and core use cases:
- Product engineers building conversational assistants that need to call backend actions (booking, search) and surface structured results to the UI.
- Platform teams that want observability over tool usage and schema compliance.
- ISVs building composable features (tools + model) for customers who require predictable outputs.

High-level API model (strawman):
- The session concept: a single long-lived interaction represented by a session_id. Client opens a realtime channel (WebSocket or HTTP/2) to /v1/realtime/sessions -> server responds with session metadata.
- Stream events (prototype event names):
  - "input_chunk": partial tokens from the user or system (client->server).
  - "model_token": streamed tokens emitted by the model (server->client).
  - "tool_request": model requests to invoke a tool (server->client). Payload: {tool_id, args, schema_hint}.
  - "tool_response": tool result (client->server after external call performed by integrator or by Redwood managed adapter if enabled).
  - "structured_output": final validated result with schema id and payload.
  - "error" / "info" events for diagnostics.

Tool calling semantics (proposal):
- Tools are registered at model invocation time via the session config. Each tool has a short capability manifest: id, name, input_schema (optional), output_schema (optional), permissions (read/write), and invocation_mode (managed|delegated).
- Invocation flow:
  1) Model emits tool_request in the stream with tool_id and input.
  2) If invocation_mode==managed and customer enabled managed adapters, Redwood proxies the call to the adapter (e.g., HTTP fetch adapter) and returns tool_response. Managed adapters are restricted and audited.
  3) If invocation_mode==delegated, the client (customer backend) receives tool_request and must call their tool and post tool_response back into the session.
  4) The model continues generation given the tool_response.
- Security: default is delegated mode (no Redwood-managed access to customer APIs) unless customer explicitly enables a managed adapter with KYC and policy checks. Tool payloads are limited in size and sanitized; tool_request events must not include secrets.

Structured output and schema validation:
- Provide a schema registry (phase 1: lightweight JSON Schema references) where models can declare the expected output schema. Each structured_output event includes schema_id, validation_status, and the payload.
- SDK helpers will surface validation errors as explicit events so the client can surface UI-level fallback (e.g., run a lint/repair pass or show a parsing error).
- Backwards compatibility: when clients don't request structured output, stream behaves as token events only.

SDK ergonomics (language-agnostic principles):
- Single abstraction: RealtimeSession object with async iterator support over events.
- Strongly-typed event objects in typed SDKs (TS/Go). In untyped SDKs (Python), provide message classes with helpers.
- Patterns to support: 
  - event.decode(): convert structured_output payload into typed object validated against schema_id.
  - session.invoke_tool(tool_id, args): convenience method that wraps sending tool_response for delegated flows.
  - auto-reconnect with resume token support: session.resume(cursor) to continue a conversation after transient network issues.
  - backpressure hints: SDK emits client-side heuristics to limit send rate to keep latency within SLO.
- Example snippet (pseudo-TS):
  const s = new RedwoodRealtimeClient().openSession({model: 'rw-infer-7b', tools: [searchTool]});
  for await (const ev of s.events()) {
    if (ev.type === 'tool_request') {
      const result = await fetchMyTool(ev.payload.args);
      await s.sendToolResponse(ev.payload.request_id, result);
    }
    if (ev.type === 'structured_output') {
      const parsed = s.schemas.decode(ev.payload.schema_id, ev.payload.data);
      render(parsed);
    }
  }

Observability and telemetry:
- New telemetry events: tool_request_count, tool_response_latency, schema_validation_failures, structured_output_rate, stream_disconnects, resume_success_rate.
- Expose per-session dashboards in Console: per-route breakdowns, token/payload counts, top tools invoked, and schema validation heatmaps.
- Logging: tool_request and tool_response bodies are redacted by default; allow increased retention/audit via enterprise compliance add-on.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (prototype): internal alpha with Redwood integration teams, limited to internal datasets.
- Phase 1 (alpha): 5 external customers opt-in, delegated-only tool calling, basic schema registry, SDK preview (JS + Python).
- Phase 2 (beta): add managed adapters (HTTP, SQL read-only) behind enterprise contract, improved SDK ergonomics, Console integrations.
- Phase 3 (GA): broader availability, SLA, and extended adapters.

Metrics for success:
- Product: % of interactive customers adopting realtime sessions, fraction of sessions using structured_output, reduction in client-side parse errors.
- Reliability: p50/p95 end-to-end latency for interactive flows, session disconnect rate < 1% per day.
- Security/ops: zero incidents where managed adapters exfiltrated data; audit logs enabled for enterprise customers.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Transport: HTTP/2 streaming vs WebSocket vs gRPC-web. WebSocket easiest for browser, HTTP/2 streaming may be friendlier to existing infra. Need infra input (infra/serving-runtime) on connection scaling.
- Schema enforcement: strict validation might break existing assistants; we need a migration path with warnings and repair suggestions.
- Tool invocation ordering and backpressure: should we block model generation until tool_response arrives (simpler) or allow speculative generation (complex but lower latency)?
- Cost model: streaming + managed adapters may increase unit costs; propose separate billing for managed adapter calls and for schema validation heavy workloads.

Risks and mitigations:
- Security: tooling could be abused to probe internal endpoints. Mitigate with capability manifests, default delegation, network egress controls for managed adapters, and per-customer allowlists.
- Latency: external tool calls can add unbounded latency. Mitigate with timeouts, fallbacks to cached results, and guidance in SDK for optimistic UX patterns.
- Complexity for developers: multiple event types may be confusing. Mitigate with high-quality SDKs, examples, and a reference application.

Next steps (owners & immediate tasks):
- Product: finalize API event taxonomy and capability manifest (owner: Simone).
- Infra/Serving: spike connection scaling and resume semantics (owner: Marcus Lee).
- SDK: prototype JS async iterator + schema helper (owner: Priya Nair).
- Security: define managed adapter onboarding checklist and KYC requirements (owner: Evan Thompson).
- QA: define test harness for schema validation and tool flows (owner: Jordan Wu).

Appendix - quick notes and links:
- Related tickets: JIRA-API-1021 (customer requests), JIRA-SERV-744 (connection scaling), JIRA-SEC-512 (adapter security).
- Slack threads: #prod-hosted-api realtime-discuss (thread id 4523).
- Reference: prior doc "hosted-streaming-sdk-proposal-draft" exists; this doc refactors around a session/event model and adds tool-calling and structured output as first-class primitives.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working draft. Expect many concrete changes to the event payload shapes and schema registry design. Please comment on the event taxonomy and the proposed default security posture (delegated-first, managed-on-request).
- Questions to specifically answer in review: preferred transports, billing model for managed adapter calls, and SDK language priority for alpha.

End of doc.
